name: Psoriatic Arthritis

prevalence.estimate: 0.05% to 0.25% of the general population; 6-42% of psoriasis patients

ethnicAssociations: Parallels psoriasis prevalence: more common in Northern European populations
Less common in Asian and African populations

diagnosticCriteria.formalCriteriaName: CASPAR Criteria (Classification Criteria for Psoriatic Arthritis, 2006)

criteria.description: Established inflammatory articular disease (joint, spine, or entheseal)
Personal history of psoriasis (if no current psoriasis; scores 1 point)
Family history of psoriasis (if no personal history; scores 1 point)
Typical psoriatic nail dystrophy (pitting, onycholysis, hyperkeratosis; scores 1 point)
Current dactylitis or history of dactylitis (scores 1 point)
Radiographic evidence of juxta-articular new bone formation on hand/foot X-ray (scores 1 point)

diagnosticCriteria.minimumForDiagnosis: Inflammatory articular disease PLUS >= 3 points from the CASPAR criteria categories. Sensitivity 91.4%, specificity 98.7%.
diagnosticCriteria.notes: Psoriasis may precede arthritis by years; in ~15% of cases arthritis precedes psoriasis onset.

pathognomonic.notes: Diffuse swelling of an entire digit; highly characteristic of PsA among arthritides

pathognomonic.symptomName: Psoriatic nail changes with concurrent joint inflammation
pathognomonic.notes: Nail pitting, onycholysis, subungual hyperkeratosis associated with DIP joint disease

common.notes: Usually precedes arthritis; check hidden areas (scalp, navel, gluteal cleft)
DIP joint predominant pattern relatively specific to PsA

occasional.notes: Often asymmetric sacroiliitis; may have bulky non-marginal syndesmophytes
Rare but devastating; telescoping digits (opera glass hand)

occasional.symptomName: Nail pitting and onycholysis without joint disease

rare.notes: Extremely rare; associated with longstanding uncontrolled inflammation

laboratory: Elevated ESR and CRP during active disease
Elevated uric acid in some patients (can mimic gout)
HLA-B27 positive in 20-50% (especially with axial involvement)
imaging: Radiographs: Pencil-in-cup deformity, juxta-articular new bone formation (periostitis), asymmetric joint space narrowing
Asymmetric sacroiliitis on pelvic radiograph or MRI
Ultrasound: Enthesitis with power Doppler signal
MRI: Bone marrow edema, enthesitis, synovitis, dactylitis
genetic: IL-23R, TNIP1, and other psoriasis susceptibility loci
other: DAPSA (Disease Activity in Psoriatic Arthritis) score
MDA (Minimal Disease Activity) criteria for treatment targets

distinguishingFeatures: AS has symmetric sacroiliitis and marginal syndesmophytes
ReA lacks psoriatic skin plaques (though keratoderma blennorrhagica can mimic)
hEDS has hypermobility not inflammatory arthritis
hEDS lacks psoriasis and nail changes

redFlags: Rapidly progressive joint destruction (arthritis mutilans pattern)
Severe, widespread skin disease unresponsive to treatment
New eye symptoms (uveitis requiring urgent ophthalmology)
Constitutional symptoms (fever, weight loss) suggesting overlap or complication
references: Taylor W, et al. Classification criteria for psoriatic arthritis: development of new criteria from a large international study. Arthritis Rheum. 2006;54(8):2665-73.
Ritchlin CT, Colbert RA, Gladman DD. Psoriatic arthritis. N Engl J Med. 2017;376(10):957-70.
Coates LC, et al. Group for Research and Assessment of Psoriasis and Psoriatic Arthritis (GRAPPA): updated treatment recommendations 2021. Nat Rev Rheumatol. 2022;18(8):465-79.
Gladman DD, et al. Psoriatic arthritis: epidemiology, clinical features, course, and outcome. Ann Rheum Dis. 2005;64(Suppl 2):ii14-17.
